prohibited_recommendations: Do not give scheduled or long-acting benzodiazepines; treat alcohol withdrawal symptom-triggered with the lowest effective dose of lorazepam or oxazepam and close monitoring of consciousness (EASL ALD 2018).
Do not prescribe opioids or other sedating drugs: they precipitate and prolong HE; for pain use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day.
Do not delay antibiotics for SBP while waiting for culture results.
Do not use co-trimoxazole for SBP prophylaxis: documented sulfonamide allergy.
required_recommendations: Treat SBP with IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily (or cefotaxime), adjusted to culture, plus albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3; repeat paracentesis at 48 hours if there is no clinical improvement (EASL 2018).
Blood, urine and ascitic cultures are drawn before the first antibiotic dose, which is not delayed for them.

Lactulose 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least two soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022); avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury.
Restart rifaximin 550 mg twice daily with lactulose to prevent recurrence (ACG 2026; EASL 2022), with a supply plan so that the prescription does not lapse again.
Give parenteral thiamine before any glucose (recent drinking, poor oral intake).
After this SBP episode, start long-term secondary prophylaxis with a fluoroquinolone (norfloxacin 400 mg daily or ciprofloxacin); co-trimoxazole is excluded by his sulfonamide allergy (EASL 2018).
Monitor blood pressure and creatinine daily (creatinine 1.4 with SBP), and reduce or hold propranolol if systolic pressure falls below 90 mmHg or acute kidney injury develops (Baveno VII).
Monitor for alcohol withdrawal (last drink the day before admission); once he recovers, offer treatment for alcohol use disorder with abstinence support (EASL ALD 2018).
Refer for liver transplant assessment: decompensated cirrhosis with overt HE, MELD-Na 28, treated HCC; the alcohol relapse is part of that assessment (EASL 2018).

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.
FDG PET has no role in HE workup; metabolic encephalopathy is reversible with precipitant control and does not require nuclear functional imaging.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade III), alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 28) with treated HCC, precipitated by spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (ascitic PMN 310 cells/mm3), rifaximin non-adherence and recent alcohol use.

differential.diagnosis: Sepsis-associated encephalopathy from SBP as the sole cause
differential.key_features: SBP is confirmed (ascitic PMN 310) and contributes, but asterixis, fetor hepaticus, a prior HE episode and the rifaximin gap in decompensated cirrhosis make HE the main mechanism; both are treated together.

Last drink the day before; tachycardia and agitation can reflect early withdrawal, but asterixis and fetor favor HE. Intoxication is excluded by ethanol 14 mg/dL. Monitor; withdrawal may emerge over the next 48-72 hours.
INR 2.2, platelets 62 and recent alcohol raise the risk, but there is no focal deficit or known head injury and CT shows no hemorrhage.
Chronic alcohol use places him at risk; no ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus; give parenteral thiamine before glucose regardless.
Solitary 1.8 cm HCC treated with TACE; no focal deficit; CT shows no mass. MRI only if the course is atypical.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grade, evidence of liver disease and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).
Child-Pugh C (14: bilirubin 5.2 3, albumin 2.1 3, INR 2.2 2, moderate ascites 3, HE grade III 3); MELD-Na 28 (creatinine 1.4, bilirubin 5.2, INR 2.2, sodium 130).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleeding, electrolyte disturbance, constipation, sedatives, alcohol, dehydration and renal failure.
Infection, especially SBP, is the commonest precipitant of overt HE in decompensated cirrhosis with ascites and may present without fever; diagnostic paracentesis is mandatory (EASL 2018).
Rifaximin non-adherence is an under-recognized but common precipitant of overt HE in patients on secondary prophylaxis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Ethanol 14 mg/dL is far too low to cause grade III encephalopathy; asterixis, fetor and the confirmed SBP (PMN 310) with the rifaximin gap make this HE precipitated by SBP. Recent drinking matters for withdrawal monitoring and thiamine, not as the explanation.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute grade III obtundation to acute alcohol intoxication and adopt 'wait it out' management.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A solitary treated HCC and no focal deficit make a brain metastasis very unlikely; treat HE and its SBP precipitant first; MRI only if the course is atypical.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Pursue HCC progression / brain metastasis workup as primary cause of AMS.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. B. is a 61-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C), prior HCC treated with TACE, and a prior HE episode 4 months ago now on rifaximin prophylaxis, brought by his daughter for acute confusion and agitation over the preceding 24 hours. His daughter reported he was found disoriented in the bathroom at 2 AM, had been slurring his speech since yesterday evening, and had been combative and uncooperative throughout the morning. She found an empty vodka bottle in his room, and he admitted on direct questioning to having drunk 'a little yesterday.' He had last been seen by hepatology 3 weeks ago when labs showed stable MELD 18. Over the prior week, his daughter noticed decreasing oral intake, reduced rifaximin adherence (ran out 5 days ago and had not refilled), and increasing abdominal distension. He denied hematemesis or melena. Temperature on arrival was 37.9°C.
